What Needs You
Show Everything

What Needs You is where the world tells you things and asks you things. A notice says what happened: groceries you couldn’t pay for, a commitment you slept through, a welcome to the school. A question carries its answers as buttons, such as File It or Keep The Account, and Dismiss. The number beside Home on the menu is how many of both are waiting.

Where To Find It
Home, The What Needs You Panel.
When You Can Use It
From “What Needs You”.
Show Me Where
What To Press
Open Home and read What Needs You: questions first, then notices.
Press one of a question’s answers to act on it there. It does what the same button on its own screen does.
Press Go There to open the screen a question or a notice is about.
Press Dismiss to take a question off the list without answering it.
Press Mark N Read, at the top of the panel, to mark every unread notice read at once.
Press Show All N, under the notices, to see every unread one before you do: the panel draws the six most important first, and Show The Six Most Important goes back to them.
Press a question’s or a notice’s title to open it: how urgent or important it is, when it closes, and where it sits in the list.

DRAM 163a · Due November 3, 2027 · Skills: Script Analysis

How This Works
The Impostures of Scapin, Molière, tr. Charles Heron Wall (1671), Act Three, Scene Two, a street in Naples: the sack: you play Scapin. Géronte has paid Scapin five hundred crowns to ransom his son from a Turkish galley, and he told his son that Scapin had betrayed him, which put Scapin on his knees under Léandre’s sword confessing his own tricks. Now Scapin has his revenge. He tells the old man that the brother of Octave’s bride and his friends, men of the sword, hold every street to his house, and that the one way home is in a sack on Scapin’s shoulders. Géronte gets in. Scapin plays a Gascon bully who beats the sack for its master’s sake, then a foreigner who beats it when Scapin won’t show what’s inside, then half a dozen soldiers at once, crying out each time as if the blows fell on him and pushing the old man’s head back in whenever it comes out to complain. As the soldiers are about to strike, Géronte looks out quietly, sees the trick, and Scapin runs.

WHAT THE IMPOSTURES OF SCAPIN ASKS
Everyday Speech: Quick, plain prose: the period is in the situation, and what the voices ask is their accents.
Timing: Built On It. Scapin’s asides to the sack in his own voice between a bully’s lines, keeping the old man still and hidden, and each blow cried out as it falls.
Physical Work: Built On It. The sack got into, the stick laid on it again and again, the old man’s head pushed back in twice, and the run at the end.
Playing Off The Partner: Much. Line by line while Géronte is talked into the sack and each time he looks out of it; between, Scapin plays both sides of each encounter to a listener who can’t see him.
Vocal Demand: Built On It. Voices of his own besides his natural tone: a Gascon bully, a foreigner, half a dozen soldiers at once, and his cries as if beaten.
What’s Kept Hidden: Built On It. Géronte hides in a sack, and Scapin plays every enemy who beats it, each in another voice.
A Conflict Out Loud: Some. The bullies threaten and strike out loud, but they’re Scapin’s voices: he never puts his own quarrel, his revenge for the lie, to Géronte’s face before he runs.
Tone: comic, 5 transitions to play. Farce throughout: a miser beaten in a sack by the servant who tricked him.
Techniques It Asks: Comedy, Accents And Dialects. The bullies’ accents are written into the lines, “Vat! I shall not hab de pleasure to kill dis Géronte,” and the beating is played for its laughs.

Chase refuses to authorize any transaction once a card is reported lost or stolen, and sends a replacement card with a new number; for a credit card the account itself stays open and keeps its age for credit reporting.

Chase monitors cards around the clock and may contact the customer by text message, push notification, email or phone call to confirm whether unusual activity was authorized; fraud alerts are automatic and need no enrollment. Chase can refuse to authorize a transaction it reasonably believes may be fraudulent, but doesn’t say it holds a payment pending the customer's reply.

The law on the debit card: Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act's Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.6(b), a consumer who reports a lost or stolen debit card within two business days of learning of it owes at most the lesser of $50 or the transfers made before notice; after two business days the cap rises to $500. Transfers shown on a periodic statement that aren't reported within 60 days of the statement being sent carry unlimited liability for transfers after that 60-day window. The 2- and 60-day clocks run from different starts: learning of the loss, and the statement's transmittal.

The law on the credit card: Truth in Lending Act, Regulation Z, 12 CFR 1026.12(b)(1)(ii): a cardholder's liability for unauthorized credit card use is capped at the lesser of $50 or the amount obtained before the card issuer is notified.

The law on a payment you report as not yours: Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.11: the bank must decide within 10 business days (20 for a new account's first 30 days); if it takes longer it must provisionally credit the account within 10 business days and may take up to 45 days, or 90 days for point-of-sale debit card, out-of-state or new-account transfers. OPT gives you up to twelve months to work in your field, from the later of your program’s end and the approval, with no more than 90 days without work in total.
